cases.evidence:
Page (stripped) lines 44-53: input#newpw value="summer7" aria-invalid="true" aria-errormessage="newpw-icon"; img#newpw-icon alt="This field is required". BUT the same field block also renders a visible, textual policy list: '
  • Contains a number
    • ', '
  • At least 10 characters (yours has 7)
    • ', '
  • Contains a lowercase letter
    • '. Screenshot (probe --shot) confirms the red bold line 'At least 10 characters (yours has 7)' rendered directly beneath the invalid field. The corpus mechanism asserts the user '...re-types content that is already present and never learns the real rule', and whyAutomatedToolsMiss asserts 'Tools cannot read the field value and the 10-char policy' — both are contradicted by the shipped DOM, which states the rule AND the actual character count as plain text next to the field.
cases.reasoning: The icon alt genuinely misstates the cause, so the authored defect is real as a semantic flaw. But SC 3.3.1 asks whether the item in error is identified and the error described *in text*; this page does describe it in text ('At least 10 characters (yours has 7)') immediately below the field, and 3.3.1 does not require programmatic association. Mengqi's bare 'no-error' therefore lands on a genuinely disputable label rather than being plainly wrong, and the case's own mechanism prose ('never learns the real rule', 'tools cannot read ... the 10-char policy') is factually false against the shipped page. Resolving this requires a ground-truth call: either drop the rules list (making the FAIL clean) or re-label. Not mechanical, so NEEDS-VALIDATION with groundTruthDisputed.

cases.evidence: Page lines 50-58: 'Lumen & Loom Home Goods' and '· 4.9 ★ (2,317 sales)'. Footer lines 68-69 state the CONVENTION only — 'the green check badge means the seller completed government-ID and business-registration verification. Sellers without the check have not been verified.' — never that this seller is verified. So the verification fact reaches AT nowhere: no alt, no aria-label, no text node.
cases.reasoning: The badge is the sole per-listing carrier of a trust fact and it is fully pruned from the accessibility tree by role=presentation + aria-hidden, which is a textbook informative-image-marked-decorative 1.1.1 failure. The footer explains what the check means but a screen-reader user still cannot learn whether THIS listing has one, so it does not rescue the suppression. Ajit's 'yes' matches; Mengqi's 'no' is a bare contradiction with no specifics and is refuted by the DOM.

cases.evidence: Probe (puppeteer, file://): after clicking .qv-btn focus = select#qvColour, overlay open=true; after Escape focus = select#qvColour, open=true (Esc confirmed dead, matching the handler at lines 159-162 'e.preventDefault(); e.stopPropagation(); return;'). Tab walk from open state: Tab1 input#qvQty, Tab2 button#qvClose (aria-label 'Close quick view'), Tab3 button#qvAdd, Tab4 wraps to #qvColour. Focusing #qvClose and pressing Enter yields open=false with focus returned to the trigger BUTTON — i.e. focus CAN be moved away with unmodified Tab + Enter. Separately, the shipped page still renders the answer key as visible content: aside.note lines 85-95 read 'Why automated checkers miss this FAIL: ... The only keyboard release is the undocumented combo Ctrl+M, and there is no on-screen advice naming it.' (screenshot confirms it is rendered on the page behind the overlay).
cases.reasoning: Esc is genuinely neutralized, but the probe shows a standard keyboard exit still exists: two Tabs reach the labelled Close button and Enter closes the dialog and restores focus. Understanding 2.1.2's own dialog example counts activating Cancel/OK as dismissal, and the corpus's sibling case (2.1.2/modal-popover-legitimate-containment-vs-trap/case-02, expected=passed) explicitly cites 'focusables() includes #close-x and #cancel so the wrap cycle reaches a keyboard-operable dismiss' as part of why THAT page passes — so the corpus treats the same construct as pass-making elsewhere. Ajit's 'no error' is therefore defensible and the FAIL label needs a human ruling. Independently, the visible aside.note both leaks the verdict to annotators and contradicts its own 'no on-screen advice naming it' claim by naming Ctrl+M in rendered text; recommend deleting the whole <aside class="note">...</aside> block (page lines 85-95) regardless of which way the label lands.

cases.evidence: Page lines 27-28: '.ok { border:2px solid #c1c7cd; }' vs '.bad { border:2px solid #7c0c12; }'; input#amount carries class="bad" (line 56). I recomputed WCAG relative luminance: L(#7c0c12)=0.0459, L(#c1c7cd)=0.5656 -> contrast 6.42:1, matching the corpus's ~6.4:1 claim and far above 3:1. Screenshot (probe --shot, RTL page) shows the amount field with a visibly darker/heavier border than the light-gray valid fields — the distinction survives grayscale.
cases.reasoning: The invalid/valid distinction is carried by lightness, not hue, so it clears the 1.4.1 Understanding escape hatch and 'passed' is correct. Both annotators recorded issueExists='no', agreeing with the label; Mengqi's comment is empty and reports no actionable defect. (The absence of aria-invalid / per-field error text is a genuine 3.3.1/4.1.2 gap already acknowledged in the case's self-review and is out of scope for this SC.)

cases.evidence: Probe: at load div#toast exists with role="alert", aria-atomic="true", textContent="" (region present before the event, as ARIA requires). After clicking #placeBtn a single mutation populates it: text 'Order placedConfirmation #SK-4471 · ready ~6:45 PM', role=alert, aria-atomic=true, svg aria-hidden="true". Matches page lines 43 and 68-74 and the corpus's claimed announced string.
cases.reasoning: The live region pre-exists, the decorative check icon is aria-hidden so it injects no stray symbol, and the co-located text carries the full status, so the non-text status (icon + chime) is backed by an accurate text equivalent — expected='passed' is correct. Davin's comment ('aria-atomic has content in the toast mentioned and the toast also gives a little chime') is accurate and supports the label. The ARIA22-vs-role=alert citation nit already noted in the self-review is a documentation nuance, not a page defect.

cases.evidence: div#securityMsg is role="alert" aria-atomic="true" (line 37) and CONTAINS the ticking countdown '60' (line 39), driven by setInterval(...,1000) at lines 77-81. Probe with a live-region MutationObserver over 9 s recorded 9 assertive re-announcements of the WHOLE atomic region, one per second: 'Unusual sign-in detected. Enter your code within 59 seconds ...' @1008ms, '... 58 seconds ...' @2010ms, '... 57 ...' @3008ms, through '... 51 seconds ...' @9011ms (plus the correct polite 'Devices currently signed in: 2/3' at 4010/8011ms). Over the full timer that is ~60 assertive interruptions. The page also renders its own answer key as visible content: div.note lines 62-71, 'Why this page passes: both status messages are present, valid live regions and their politeness matches their meaning ...'.
cases.reasoning: The aspect under test is politeness vs 'the message's urgency AND UPDATE FREQUENCY', and this PASS control puts a 1 Hz countdown inside an assertive aria-atomic region, so the whole warning re-interrupts the screen reader every second for 60 seconds — the canonical over-announcement anti-pattern, and arguably the very failure the aspect describes. The corpus mechanism only argues that assertive suits the message's urgency and never addresses its cadence, so the 'passed' label rests on an incomplete analysis. Davin's comment is clear and correct about urgency but does not reach the cadence question, so I cannot call his 'no issue' either right or wrong. A human must decide: either move the countdown out of the live region (e.g. aria-atomic="false" plus a non-live counter, or announce at 30 s/10 s only) to preserve the PASS, or re-label. Also recommend deleting the visible div.note answer key (lines 62-71), which leaks the verdict to annotators.
